📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mark Noble has called on West Ham United supporters to help transform the London Stadium into an intimidating venue as Scott Parker prepares for his first home match in charge against Preston North End.
  • Speaking in an interview with the club’s official website, Noble praised the ‘extraordinary’ loyalty of West Ham fans following relegation and insisted that the club’s ambition remains an immediate return to the Premier League.
  • In a recent development, he also challenged supporters to make life uncomfortable for visiting teams, arguing that a crowd of 60,000 should give West Ham a significant advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mark Noble has called on West Ham United supporters to help transform the London Stadium into an intimidating venue as Scott Parker prepares for his first home match in charge against Preston North End.

Speaking in an interview with the club’s official website, Noble praised the ‘extraordinary’ loyalty of West Ham fans following relegation and insisted that the club’s ambition remains an immediate return to the Premier League.

In a recent development, he also challenged supporters to make life uncomfortable for visiting teams, arguing that a crowd of 60,000 should give West Ham a significant advantage. But I think it’s notable to point out that getting the fans onside and creating an intimidating atmosphere are probably two very different things.

There’s no doubt about it. When the London Stadium is loud, it is impressive, as anybody who attended that incredible night against Sevilla will testify.

But I do think it’s a long way from being intimidating.

For that to happen, I firmly believe supporters need to be close to the pitch.

Not just to cause opposition players discomfort, but to put pressure on referees and give West Ham the kind of home advantage that seems prevalent throughout the league.

The distance between the stands and the playing surface remains a fundamental problem, regardless of how many supporters are in attendance.

It’s something I’ve previously argued when discussing proposals to improve the stadium atmosphere.

Isolated tiers in the stadium and poor pitch proximity do little to help the atmosphere at the London Stadium.

It was always my concern that relegation to the Championship would see visiting teams regard a trip to the London Stadium as a lovely day out in opulent surroundings. Opposition changing rooms are grand and palatial and their team coach can pull into the venue untroubled by home fans.

And our results in Stratford have certainly done little to disprove that theory. However, that doesn’t mean things can’t improve.

I genuinely believe that getting West Ham playing on the front foot will help eliminate some of the eerie silences we’ve heard so frequently at the London Stadium.

Noble wants supporters to see a team giving everything, and I think he’s absolutely right about that.

If Parker can produce an aggressive, attacking side that gives the crowd something to get excited about, the atmosphere should improve considerably.

But turning the London Stadium into a genuinely intimidating venue is another matter entirely.

And unfortunately, that’s a problem which can’t be solved simply by asking 60,000 people to make more noise.

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 14:27.

Tottenham Hotspur have shared footage of Lucas Bergvall and Savio back in training ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Ipswich Town.

The pair have both missed each of Spurs' last four Premier League matches, having picked up injuries ahead of October's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City.

Savio has been dealing with a muscular problem, while Bergvall has been nursing a knee injury, but Roberto De Zerbi expressed hope that the pair would return following the November international break.

On Friday, Spurs posted a 55-second clip on social media showing Savio and Bergvall in training with their teammates, taking part in warm-up exercises and drills with the ball at their feet.

According to recent reports, sávio and Bergvall in training ? ? @Betano_UK https://t.co/3Iug9LlBjf.

De Zerbi then confirmed at his pre-game press conference that the Brazilian attacker and Swedish midfielder are fine to feature against Ipswich, as well as assuring that James Maddison is fit and ready.

However, none of Mykhaylo Mudryk, Tosin Adarabioyo or Mathys Tel will be ready just yet, as the latter is still feeling the effects of the crunching tackle from Jayden Bogle in the 1-0 loss to Leeds United two weekends ago.

"Bergvall, Maddison and Savio are back," De Zerbi said. "Tosin and Mathys Tel no. Tosin is already okay but it is not the right moment to take any risks and Mathys Tel, we need another two or three weeks. Mudryk is not ready yet.".

With Tel sidelined for another two or three weeks, the Frenchman could miss each of Tottenham's next four matches, including the North London derby against Arsenal on December 6.

The Lilywhites will also have to cope without the attacker against Sunderland and Fulham on November 29 and December 3 respectively, and it also remains to be seen if Mudryk will be fit for those clashes after the Chelsea loanee burned bridges with a few Tottenham fans.

In a recent interview, Mudryk reflected on his yearning to join Tottenham's bitter rivals Arsenal in 2024, before Chelsea won the race to sign him from Shakhtar Donetsk.

It has been revealed that "Before going to Chelsea, I wanted to join Arsenal. It’s no secret,” Mudryk Ukrainian podcast Guest of Gordon. "Arsenal were the club I wanted to play for, and moving to the Emirates Stadium was my dream.

“There weren’t even any attempts to make my dream come true and move to Arsenal. The attempts from my previous agent were only to earn more money. But at the time, I didn’t know about it. I only understood about the commission and all the rest later on.".

While De Zerbi admitted he could understand Tottenham fans' frustrations, he leapt to the defence of his long-term colleague, adding: "Yes I can understand but Mudryk is a good guy, a good player, he suffered a lot with the situation in the last couple of years. He has to do one thing, show on the pitch his qualities.".

Tottenham head into the weekend in 11th place in the Premier League table, just three points shy of Bournemouth in seventh spot.

  • It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”.

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and stated: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”.

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

In a recent development, “I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

Sources indicate that “This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”.

Asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”.

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

According to recent reports, even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”.

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

Recent findings suggest that “If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel said. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”.

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

“I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel mentioned. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.

“It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

“So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I said, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”.

Tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he remarked: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”.

According to recent reports, on Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always said he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”.

Tuchel said that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”.

Tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

Industry observers note that it was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

“I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”.

Industry observers note that “It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

“It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”.

“The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”.

“That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a new level of pressure.”.

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

Sources indicate that again, not something anyone has remarked to me. Where is Tuchel finding these people?!

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”.

It has been revealed that tuchel notes that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

Sorry, Thomas, that’s not my experience at all. Everyone I speak to states he blew the Argentina game. This sounds a bit deluded. According to Tuchel, I must speak to 0.01 per cent of England fans....

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”.

Tuchel says he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”.

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”.

In a recent development, tuchel says he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel says the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”.

Sources indicate that tuchel states his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s important to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He says the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has noted the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

Sources indicate that no questions from the broadcasters about blowing the lead against Argentina and Tuchel’s opinion about the World Cup. Weird.

It has been revealed that ben White pulled out with an injury after being back to his best. It is unfortunately, a bit of a story for him. Josh King was very close and is on the radar.

It has been revealed that tuchel seems to be referring to notes as he speaks. He keeps looking down at a piece of paper he brought in with him.

“The door is always open through performance, behaviour and commitment.”.

Recent findings suggest that “They had a good start to the season. Now it’s a fresh competition. Some positions have injuries. Palmer has his numbers back and a point to prove. Trent was never non-selectable and comes in as a right back.”.

According to recent reports, we will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

West Ham’s veteran midfielder has been the subject of an honest interview in his home country on Czech radio coinciding with the release of his autobiography. One of the more revealing comments Tomas Soucek made concerns the pressure and the expectation of playing in front of a substantial audience – such as West Ham will undoubtedly face tomorrow as the season re-commences with a home tie at London Stadium in front of 60,000 expectant supporters.

Unlike several others, from his words it is clear that Soucek seems to thrive on the pressure and the weight of expectation upon him. As one of only a handful of medal winners still at the club from the 2023 campaign, Soucek’s experience should become a steadying influence in the dressing room even though he mostly starts games on the bench these days.

Handling the weight of expectation at London Stadium has been daunting at times.

‘Tornado Tom’ reveals that, far from letting it get to him, he actually enjoys the weight of expectation and pressure :.

Industry observers note that “Yes, obviously I feel it, but I like the pressure. Because football is always up and down, you have so many wins and so many losses – and it’s up to you how you recover from all of it.

“And I love that. As you mentioned, it’s the most watched league in the world. And West Ham’s fans are crazy – they’re the best in the league, and it’s such a historic club.

“From the first day until now, I think me and West Ham connection is as good as it could possibly be in all aspects.

“And, yes, the pressure is there, but I try to work with it – and that’s why we play football.” (englishradio.cz).

Industry observers note that the pressure will be significantly eased with a clean sheet and three points tomorrow – whether Soucek now, 31 gets into the action or simply acts as a calming figure in the dressing room. He is one of those very rare characters in the West Ham team – a leader on and off the pitch – and in another era could have spent years as the club’s captain.

#83902. Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 64m • 📚 Deep Dive (12749 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 64 min read (12749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~64 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution1,2,3,4.
  • Recent findings suggest that pokkesviricetes is a class of eukaryotic viruses with large, linear double-stranded DNA genomes within the phylum Nucleocytoviricota.
  • The evolutionary trajectory of nucleocytoviruses leading to the emergence of animal-infecting poxviruses remains enigmatic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution1,2,3,4. They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals5,6. Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes7, and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology8. Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of Trichomonas vaginalis9 and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

Recent findings suggest that pokkesviricetes is a class of eukaryotic viruses with large, linear double-stranded DNA genomes within the phylum Nucleocytoviricota. The class is divided into two orders, Chitovirales (poxviruses) and Asfuvirales10. Poxviruses infect a broad diversity of animals including humans11. They include the now eradicated smallpox virus, monkeypox viruses that continue to sporadically infect humans, and molluscum contagiosum virus, causing benign tumours in immunocompromised individuals, as well as vaccinia virus, a classic model of molecular virology12,13,14. Asfuviruses infect hosts ranging from unicellular eukaryotes to animals15 and include the African swine fever virus, which causes deadly and economically notable outbreaks in pigs and boars16, as well as a wider range of viruses mostly characterized in coculture with free-living amoeba15,17 or directly from the environment (for example, from plankton) using genome-resolved metagenomics6,18,19. Apart from the few viruses of global concern, as declared by the World Health Organization, the class Pokkesviricetes is of great importance for our understanding of the diversity, ecology and evolution of eukaryotic, and in particular animal, DNA viruses20,21.

The evolutionary trajectory of nucleocytoviruses leading to the emergence of animal-infecting poxviruses remains enigmatic. Animals emerged roughly 700 million years ago22 and host a variety of symbiotic unicellular eukaryotes that for the most part reside in their digestive system23,24,25, representing prime candidates for the ancestral hosts of poxviruses. Indeed, host transition from unicellular eukaryotes to animals would be greatly facilitated by a lasting period of close interactions allowing adaptation to the internal environment of the latter. Yet decades of investigations using cultivation, PCR surveys, serology and metagenomics indicated that nucleocytoviruses are mainly transient and thus rarely abundant in the digestive system of humans and other animals5,6,26. Until now, not a single group of Nucleocytoviricota was found to be commonly associated with or prevalent in the digestive system, contrasting with the broad distribution and remarkable diversity of these viruses in the environment4,6,27. With no evidence of nucleocytoviruses systematically infecting unicellular eukaryotes inside animals, early steps surrounding the emergence of poxviruses could not be explained.

It has been revealed that here we explored the global diversity and distribution of Pokkesviricetes by surveying tens of thousands of metagenomic assemblies from a broad range of environmental samples and animal-associated microbiomes. We discovered a third Pokkesviricetes order that we propose naming Egovirales. Egoviruses have large genomes and are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids. They are the closest relatives of poxviruses and almost exclusively occur in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals worldwide. One egovirus population is estimated to be present in more than 1% of the human population across continents. Highly conserved homologues of egovirus core genes were identified in genomes of Trichostomatia (ciliates), Parabasalia (Metamonada, including the pathogen Trichomonas vaginalis) and Parabasalia-associated polintons, another lineage of DNA viruses that integrate into the host genomes28, suggestive of a long history of interactions between egoviruses and these animal-associated unicellular eukaryotes. Egoviruses are among the most prevalent eukaryotic DNA viruses naturally occurring in animals. They substantially expand the evolutionary scope of Pokkesviricetes and provide critical insights into the emergence of poxviruses, pointing to anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes prevalent in the digestive system as an ancestral replicative niche that favoured host transition to animal cells.

DNA-dependent RNA polymerases are evolutionarily informative gene markers present in most viruses of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota, including all Pokkesviricetes10,29. We used a comprehensive hidden Markov model for the largest RNA polymerase subunit A (RNApolA)29,30 to search 85,123 metagenomic assemblies covering a wide range of environmental samples as well as thousands of samples from the digestive systems of humans, livestock and wild animals (Supplementary Table 1). This search identified 1,969,342 RNApolA genes, which we linked to main cellular and viral taxa using a custom reference database (Methods). Among the Pokkesviricetes, we identified a single poxvirus most closely related to Eptesipox occurring in the gut microbiome of a marsupial carnivore from Australia31, as well as 240 asfuviruses occurring only in the environment, predominantly in aquatic ecosystems (Supplementary Table 1). These results are in line with the current knowledge of the global niche partitioning of Pokkesviricetes and contribute, alongside previous metagenomic surveys6,19, to the great expansion of the known diversity of asfuviruses in the environment.

In addition to poxviruses and asfuviruses, we identified a clade of previously undescribed DNA viruses, related to these two viral orders, that were prevalent in the digestive system and which we provisionally name egoviruses. We characterized 12 complete, non-redundant egovirus genomes (average nucleotide identity less than 98%) from the digestive systems of humans, buffalo, goats, chicken, deer and pigs. These linear genomes are 160–360 kilobases (kb) in length and contain 55 base pair (bp) inverted terminal repeats, a feature characteristic of Pokkesviricetes32,33. The egovirus genomes encompass all eight Nucleocytoviricota hallmark genes10,29 (Supplementary Table 2), with the family B DNA polymerase (DNApolB) coding region often split into two separate open reading frames, echoing trans-splicing of another critical gene (the terminase) recently discovered in mirusviruses34. We built an hidden Markov model for the egovirus double-jelly-roll-major capsid protein (DJR-MCP) to complement the RNApolA survey and further expanded the search for egoviruses across metagenomes. Overall, we identified egovirus RNApolA and/or DJR-MCP in 864 metagenomic assemblies (detection of both markers in 286 samples), mainly from digestive systems of a wide range of animals (Supplementary Table 2). The mean coverage in these 864 egovirus-positive metagenomes was roughly 10× for the egovirus RNApolA and roughly 15× for the egovirus major capsid protein (MCP) (R2 = 0.89), reaching more than 100× in some of the human, buffalo, pig and chicken samples (Supplementary Table 2). Using these 2 marker genes, we recovered more than 200 metagenome-assembled genomes in addition to the 12 complete genomes (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Information). Egovirus genomes were on average 81% complete (minimal quality score of 50%; Methods) and were up to 467 kb in size (mean of 229 kb). Phylogenetic analysis of manually curated hallmark proteins confidently identified egoviruses as a distinct main clade within the class Pokkesviricetes that is most closely related to poxviruses (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1). On the basis of these findings, egoviruses should represent a third order within Pokkesviricetes that we propose naming Egovirales. Egovirales is the only clade within the phylum Nucleocytoviricota found to be commonly present in the digestive system.

a, A maximum-likelihood phylogenomic analysis of members of Nucleocytoviricota, along with 202 Egovirales genomes with a quality score above 50%. The tree covers 1,807 genomes and was built using concatenated multiple alignments of four hallmark proteins of Nucleocytovoricota (DNApolB, RNApolA, RNApolB and transcription factor IIS; 4,110 sites) using IQ-TREE with the LG+F+R10 model. The tree was rooted with the putative class Proculviricetes and visualized using anvi’o v.9.1. Green dots in the tree highlight high supports for key nodes (approximate likelhood ratio ≥ 80 and ultrafast bootstrap approximation ≥ 95; Methods). b, Structural modelling of an Egovirales DJR-MCP (human main clade) (bottom) and comparison to the structures of DJR-MCPs from three reference Pokkesviricetes DJR-MCPs (Protein Data Bank codes from top to second from bottom: 3SAM, 6KU9 and 5J7O). The panel also indicates box plots summarizing variation in protein length for the DJR-MCPs of egoviruses (complete genomes), faustoviruses, other clades of asfuviruses and Chitovirales. Centre lines in box plots show the medians; box limits indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles; whiskers extend 1.5 times the interquartile range from the 25th and 75th percentiles; all data points are visualized as individual dots. c, Gene flux signal between orders of nucleocytoviruses and eight eukaryotic genera (only the best hits are considered).

Recent findings suggest that we identified 57 core genes represented in at least 10 of the 12 complete Egovirales genomes and functionally annotated most of them by sequence analysis and structural modelling (Methods and Supplementary Table 3). These core genes encompass key functionalities of nucleocytoviruses6,19,30 and include a histone doublet that we propose is involved in genome condensation into nucleosome-like structures. Histones, including histone doublets, have been previously described in some members of the Nucleocytoviricota, in particular, marseilleviruses35,36 and medusaviruses37, but not in members of Pokkesviricetes38. Egoviruses encode the main proteins involved in virion morphogenesis that are conserved across Nucleocytoviricota, including poxviruses and asfuviruses. The core components of this module are the DJR-MCP (Fig. 1), the A32-like genome packaging ATPase and the Ulp1-like capsid maturation protease. The Egovirales DJR-MCPs are unusually large (average of 806 amino acids among the complete Egovirales genomes) and the region facing the exterior of the capsid is highly diversified among egoviruses (Extended Data Fig. 2). These trends echo previous observations on the large MCPs of faustoviruses from the order Asfuvirales17. In addition, egoviruses encode homologues of the main virion proteins exclusive to asfuviruses, namely, structural polyproteins pp220 and pp62 (Supplementary Information). In African swine fever virus, both polyproteins are processed into many structural proteins that play crucial roles in the formation of multilayered capsids39,40. Collectively, the presence of these structural proteins strongly suggests that egoviruses form icosahedral multilayered capsids that are similar to those of Asfuvirales41, but differ from both the icosahedral capsids of most nucleocytoviruses and the brick-shaped virions of poxviruses42.

We used RNApolA and/or DJR-MCP genes of Egovirales found in metagenomic assemblies to perform a global survey of the occurrence and diversity of egoviruses (Supplementary Table 2). Both phylogenies include the same six human-specific egovirus clades (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2). Five of these clades are specific to human gut samples, whereas the last one (clade 03) only occurred in human saliva samples. Only nine egovirus-like RNApolA genes were retrieved from environmental samples, including an aquifer, a cold seep and marine sediments (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1). In the phylogenetic tree, these sequences formed four small clades, two of which (from marine sediments) were the most basal branches of Egovirales. All the remaining RNApolA sequences (more than 97% of the data) originated from the digestive system, representing the bulk of known Egovirales diversity. The DJR-MCP phylogeny recapitulated these trends, with more than 99% of the sequences, in this case, originating from the digestive system (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Recent findings suggest that a, A maximum-likelihood phylogeny of the RNApolA of egoviruses (n = 324), using representatives of Chitovirales and Asfuvirales for rooting (1,357 sites), and the LG+F+R7 model. The layers of information summarize the ecosystem type (environment (Env) versus human versus other animals) as well as selections corresponding to egovirus clades occurring in the same animal species. The six human-specific clades are also highlighted. A similar analysis focused on the MCP of egoviruses is presented in Extended Data Fig. 3. B rat, bamboo rat. b, The prevalence for Egovirales (using signal from both the RNApolA and MCP surveys) in cohorts of metagenomic assemblies corresponding to different animal species. c, The 864 egovirus-positive samples that correspond to one of the six human-specific clades.

Industry observers note that we surveyed 11,788 metagenomes with at least 5 million reads from 26 gut-related bioprojects (17 of them cover humans) to estimate the prevalence of egoviruses in animal species (Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Information). Egovirus hallmark genes were detected in the digestive system of humans of various age and geographic location (n = 193; 2.3% of egovirus-positive samples), with a notable increase of signal among hunter-gatherers from Tanzania43 (the Hadza; 6.2% of egovirus-positive samples) (Fig. 2). This enhanced signal is due to higher egovirus diversity rather than a higher prevalence of the most prevalent human clade (clade 01; just 3.1% of egovirus-positive samples). Notably, three human-specific egovirus clades were detected (almost) exclusively in the Hadza hunter-gatherers (clades 02, 04 and 05), suggesting that lifestyle could affect the diversity of human-associated egoviruses. Egoviruses were also well represented in the digestive system of pigs (n = 155; 11% of egovirus-positive samples), buffalo (n = 182; 26%), goats (n = 69; 14%), cows (n = 31; 7.8%) and chicken (n = 38; 11%). To a lesser extent, egoviruses were detected in other livestock for which fewer samples were available (deer, yak, sheep, zebu and reindeer) (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Similar percentages of egovirus-positive samples (for example, 2.7% for human versus 29% for buffalo) were observed when only considering metagenomes containing between 50 million and 200 million reads (n = 4,909) to minimize sequencing depth variations (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Information). Buffalo had by far the highest Egovirales prevalence among the surveyed animal species, with viruses covering a wide range of distantly related clades (Fig. 2) and prevailing in the ruminant stomach compartments (Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Information). Even fewer metagenomes were available for the digestive system of wild animals, but nevertheless, bamboo rats, a golden bamboo lemur, an olive baboon and a white rhinoceros were found to be extra carriers of egoviruses, indicating that primates and other wild mammals also represent a substantial reservoir of egovirus diversity.

Industry observers note that examination of the Egovirales dispersal across all metagenomic assemblies indicates that clades of closely related egoviruses tend to occur in the same animal species. This was most apparent for the two main clades associated with humans and pigs (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3). We characterized the main human clade (clade 01) in 186 metagenomic assemblies from 19 studies that cover various countries from many continents, including Tanzania (the Hadza), Nepal, Fiji islanders, the USA, England, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Italy and Spain (Supplementary Table 2). Average amino acid identity was 99.4% among the RNApolA genes and 99.9% among the MCP genes, indicating that this clade represents a cohesive viral population occurring among humans at a global scale. A complementary k-mer survey of 3 hallmark genes from a clade 01 genomic representative against assemblies of the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) detected this viral population in more than 500 metagenomes, broadening the geographic scope of its signal within the human population (Supplementary Table 4 and Methods). Overall metagenomic signal indicates that this viral population (92% of the egovirus-positive human gut samples) is present in more than 1% of the human population (including in remote rural villages and densely populated areas44,45), encompasses various stages of the human lifespan (for example, in a 3-year-old child and a pregnant woman) and remains present over time in longitudinal studies of the same individuals46 (up to nearly 1 year of sampling). The main pig clade shared similar trends, being found in 109 metagenomic assemblies from 4 studies that cover countries from many continents. Finally, the egovirus clade characteristic of human saliva was found in the USA and Fiji47,48. These results demonstrate that cohesive egovirus populations can cover expansive geographic regions while being strictly associated with a specific body site (gut or saliva) of a single animal species. In addition, we found instances of closely related egoviruses occurring in several animal species. Examples include goat–deer, pig–cow and deer–buffalo pairs (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Overall, our results demonstrate the worldwide spread and strong co-occurrence of egovirus populations with one or more animal species.

In a recent development, repetitive infections over extended periods of time typically result in lateral gene transfers between viruses and their prime eukaryotic hosts, a signal detectable by means of comparative genomics6,49. To predict the host range of egoviruses, we performed a global protein-centric genomic comparison between nucleocytoviruses and a wide range of eukaryotic lineages (Methods). In line with their known host ranges, our results showed a strong gene flux signal between poxviruses and Chordata (chordopoxviruses) or Arthropoda (entomopoxviruses) (Fig. 1). By sharp contrast, the same analysis showed strong gene flux signal between egoviruses and two animal-associated groups of unicellular eukaryotes: phylum Parabasalia (43% of Egovirales–eukaryote gene flux) and order Trichostomatia (42%) (Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Information). This gene flux signal is effectively unique of egoviruses among the known nucleocytoviruses (Fig. 1). It is largely driven by egovirus core genes of known function (for example, DNApolB, RNA polymerase A, messenger RNA (mRNA) capping and Holliday junction resolvase) as well as egovirus core genes of unknown function (with no orthologues detected in other nucleocytoviruses), which appear to have been sporadically transferred into Parabasalia and/or Trichostomatia genomes (see Extended Data Figs. 5–7 for the corresponding phylogenetic analyses). Within Parabasalia, egoviruses were primarily linked to the genera Trichomonas and Tritrichomonas (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 5), which correspond to prevalent pathogens of humans and other animals. Within Trichostomatia, the gene flux signal was almost entirely constrained to the family Ophryoscolecidae (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 5), which is best known for its participation in digestive processes in ruminants (including buffalo)7.

Aside from Parabasalia and Trichostomatia, we did not detect any clear gene flux signal to connect egoviruses with other prevalent animal-associated unicellular eukaryotes (Supplementary Tables 5–7). The most notable case in point is Blastocystis (a stramenopile), which is widespread in the digestive system50,51,52, coexisting with egoviruses in many human, chicken and pig samples especially within the scope of our metagenomic survey (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 4), and yet reveals no gene flux to egoviruses. The complete lack of a gene flux signal for Blastocystis, despite a considerable niche overlap with egoviruses, quantified here with metagenomics, demonstrates that horizontal gene transfers are not random and do not occur between egoviruses and all co-occurring protists in the digestive system. Thus, although no direct evidence of infection of a specific host by egoviruses is available, the overall gene flux signal and the presence of homologues of egovirus core genes in reference Parabasalia and Trichostomatia genomes (Supplementary Table 8) appear to point to these protists as likely hosts of egoviruses. Parabasalia (Metamonada) and Trichostomatia (ciliates) belong to distinct phyla of unicellular eukaryotes53 that show commonalities in their lifestyle and cell biology. Specifically, both groups of unicellular eukaryotes have anaerobic lifestyle, inhabit the digestive tract of animals and can perform phagocytosis54,55, a mechanism well-known to be exploited by large DNA viruses to enter their host cells56,57.

Sources indicate that polintons correspond to a main lineage of DNA viruses with a DJR-MCP that infect a wide range of eukaryotes28. Parabasalia genomes, and especially those of T. vaginalis, contain numerous endogenous polintons encompassing roughly 20 genes9. One of these genes encode KilA, a DNA-binding protein of unknown function that appears to be restricted to polintons integrated in Parabasalia genomes58. KilA is also a core gene of poxviruses and egoviruses, with a more sporadic occurrence among other nucleocytoviruses (including within the class Megaviricetes). Our phylogenetic analysis of KilA suggests an ancient evolutionary history of this gene among the nucleocytoviruses (Fig. 3). This analysis further demonstrated that polinton KilA genes comprised two distinct clades (types I and II), with the tree topology indicating that their respective common ancestors were acquired from distinct egoviruses before the radiation of Trichomonas, Tritrichomonas and other related parabasalids from their common ancestor. In the genome of T. vaginalis strain G3 (176 Mb), the two KilA clades are represented by high copy numbers (1,116 copies of type I and 718 copies of type II) and spread across all chromosomes (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 9). The second species of Parabasalia with the highest copy number of the two clades is that of Trichomonas tenax. The apparent transfer of an egovirus core gene to polintons, endogenous viruses of Parabasalia, strengthens the connection between egoviruses and this clade of gut-associated anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes.

a, A phylogenetic analysis of KilA predicted proteins from nucleocytoviruses and endogenous polintons (2,207 sequences, 313 sites; model VT+F+R9), which delineates two phylogenetic clades (KilA types I and II) in the polintons. Only representatives of highly redundant Metamonada protein sequences (95% sequence identity) have been selected (Methods); the number of represented sequences is shown as ‘copy number’. b, The occurrence of the KilA genes across genomes of T. vaginalis strain G3. c, The genomic structure of polinton P1-TV (ref. 58) integrated into the genome of T. vaginalis strain G3. Chr., chromosome.

Our global metagenomic survey of DNA viruses of class Pokkesviricetes led to the discovery of a third putative order in this class, which we provisionally name Egovirales. Egoviruses have linear genomes that can reach 467 kb in length and occur mostly in the digestive system of humans (six clades characterized), livestock (the bulk of the characterized Egovirales diversity) and wild animals, in which they prevail worldwide. Egoviruses have a highly divergent MCP (DJR-MCP). We propose that egoviruses, which encode homologues of the main virion proteins exclusive to asfuviruses, produce viral particles with an icosahedral multilayered structure resembling the virions of African swine fever virus. Egoviruses not only fill major gaps in our knowledge of the ecology and evolution of Pokkesviricetes, but also represent the only group of viruses discovered so far with large DNA genomes that is common and detected almost only in human and animal gut microbiomes. Given its evolutionary trajectory and distribution patterns, this previously overlooked main group of viruses with complex genomes is of prime interest to human and veterinary virology as well as viral evolution.

Until now, the digestive system was considered to encompass a limited diversity and abundance of eukaryotic DNA viruses5,6,26, with the most prevalent ones, such as anelloviruses59, having small, single-stranded DNA genomes of only a few kilobases. No convincing evidence of reproduction in the gut is available for viruses of eukaryotes with large DNA genomes. But, contrasting with the other Nucleocytoviricota lineages, many lines of data challenge the hypothesis of consumed water or food being the main source of egoviruses in the digestive system of humans and animals. First, egoviruses were almost never detected in environmental samples but are projected just from the metagenomic assembly signal (in the context of animal population statistics available from the United Nations) to be present in the digestive systems of roughly 180 million humans, billions of livestock animals and chickens, as well as numerous wild animals. These viruses were discovered by metagenome analysis, an approach that only targets the most abundant viral genomes and were detected by this method alone in more than 2% of the analysed human gut microbiomes and in even higher fractions of many animal microbiomes. Among animals with the highest prevalence for Egovirales, it is projected that a substantial proportion (possibly, most) of the roughly 200 million buffalo contain 1 or many egovirus species thriving in their stomach compartments. Second, the most prevalent human-specific egovirus clade alone, found in a wide range of metagenomic surveys covering several continents, is projected to be present in the gut of more than 1% of humans. In addition, longitudinal studies indicate that this clade can remain present over long periods of time in the gut of the same human individual. Thus, egoviruses are diverse, widespread and resilient viruses prevalent in the digestive system. Finally, the occurrence of one human-specific egovirus clade characteristic of the oral cavity provides the first indication that distinct egoviruses occur broadly in more animal body sites, further indicating that egoviruses are most probably not transient, but rather long-term members of the human gut and oral cavity microbiomes.

Together, comparative genomics and targeted phylogenetic analysis (for example, of the DNApolB) provide a strong prediction of virus–host interaction between egoviruses and two distantly related groups of unicellular eukaryotes (order Trichostomatia and phylum Parabasalia) that are both anaerobic, perform phagocytosis and prevail in the digestive system and oral cavity of animals24,25,54,55,60,61,62. The Egovirales–Parabasalia linkage is mostly restricted to Trichomonas and Tritrichomonas, two genera that include prominent pathogens infecting a wide range of animals and humans and can markedly affect animal immunity8. For instance, Tritrichomonas foetus is a parasite of cattle (reproductive tract) and cats (large intestine) as well as a commensal in the stomach and gut of pigs61. In addition, T. vaginalis is the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infectious agent among humans with roughly 150 million estimated cases per year63. The notable case of the apparent egovirus-to-polinton KilA gene transfer followed by the spread of polintons across the genomes of T. vaginalis and T. tenax (parasite inhabiting the human oral cavity62) further supports the long-lasting association between egoviruses and Parabasalia. The Egovirales–Trichostomatia linkage is almost entirely restricted to genera of the family Ophryoscolecidae, known to play a central role in ruminant digestive processes7,64. High prevalence of these Trichostomatia and Parabasalia genera in animals, and their phagocytosis-centric feeding lifestyle, explain the wide spread of egoviruses across animal species and suggest a long history of egovirus replication in the digestive system.

The evolution of poxviruses in animals (covering both insects and vertebrates), including the emergence of smallpox, estimated to have killed half a billion humans over the course of a century, has been extensively studied11,65,66. However, the origin of poxviruses as a group remains enigmatic due to their distant (albeit unequivocal) relationships with other nucleocytoviruses and the lack of intermediate forms. Egoviruses provide that missing link, given their phylogenetic position as the sister clade to poxviruses and their prevalence in the digestive system. Although thus far egoviruses were detected only in mammals and chickens, this signal is affected by the availability of metagenomic sequencing data among animal species, which is at present strongly biased towards humans and livestock. The diversity of egoviruses is probably substantially undersampled, especially among wild animals. The results of this work indicate that the common ancestor of poxviruses and egoviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes capable of phagocytosis in the gut of ancestral animals before the divergence of insects and vertebrates (protostomes and deuterostomes) from their common ancestor about 700 million years ago22. Given that prominent metamonad pathogens, such as Trichomonas and Tritrichomonas, bind directly to the epithelium during infection67,68, and that pathogenic ciliates can also penetrate the animal tissue69, it is conceivable that poxviruses have evolved from an egovirus-like ancestor that gained the ability to reproduce in the animal gut epithelial cells. Our analysis of egovirus genomes suggests that the last common ancestor of Pokkesviricetes and the common ancestor of egoviruses and poxviruses had a multilayered icosahedral capsid resembling that of asfuviruses. This capsid was replaced with brick-shaped particles in the ancestors of poxviruses following their split from egoviruses and perhaps concomitantly with the invasion of animal gut epithelial cells.

According to recent reports, the out-of-the-gut evolutionary scenario for poxviruses seems to align well with the biology of both poxviruses and eukaryotes. On the viral side, entomopoxviruses can perform an early replication phase in the midgut of insects by first infecting the epithelial cells70. There is no evidence of poxvirus replication in the gut of vertebrates. On the cellular side, phagocytosis is an important component of the immune system of animals71 serving as the entry point for various DNA viruses56,57 and is also a main feeding mechanism in both metamonads72 and ciliates73. Thus, the ability of epithelial cells to perform phagocytosis74,75 offers one possible mechanistic explanation for how a DNA virus infecting anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes in the digestive system could have successfully initiated the infection of adjacent animal cells. Altogether, this work demonstrates that a distinct group of nucleocytoviruses is common in human and animal gut, in contrast to the previous belief, and sheds light on the origin of poxviruses.

Metagenomes (listed in Supplementary Table 1) were assembled and processed as part of the mOTUs database76,77,78. Here we provide details on the metagenomic assemblies for context. Briefly, BBMap79 (v.38.71) was used to quality control sequencing reads from all samples by removing adaptors from the reads, removing reads that mapped to quality control sequences (PhiX genome) and discarding low-quality reads (trimq = 14, maq = 20, maxns = 1 and minlength = 45). Quality-controlled reads were merged using bbmerge.sh with a minimum overlap of 16 bases, resulting in merged, unmerged paired and single reads. The reads from metagenomic samples were assembled into scaffolds using the SPAdes assembler80 (v.3.15.2) in metagenomic mode. Scaffolds were length-filtered (500 bp or more) and gene sequences were predicted using Prodigal81 (v.2.6.3) with the parameters -c -q -m -p meta.

In a recent development, A broad-spectrum hidden Markov model (HMM) profile for the RNApolA hallmark gene29 was searched against the predicted gene sequences from the metagenomic database using hmmsearch (HMMER82 v.3.1b2) with an E-value cutoff of 1 × 10−50. This search resulted in the identification of nearly 2 million RNApolA genes. Positive hits were then linked back to their source scaffold.

It has been revealed that we collected amino acid sequences corresponding to a broad range of reference RNApolA genes for bacterial, archaeal, eukaryotic and giant virus lineages characterized by means of cultivation and environmental genomics30,83,84. We generated a custom diamond (v.2.1.8) database85 from this resource and summarized the taxonomic affiliation of each sequence in a complementary metadata file. We then performed a diamond blast search (v.2.1.8) of RNApolA genes identified from the metagenomic survey using this custom database and exploited the associated metadata file to assess both their taxonomic affiliation and novelty score (based on the percentage identity).

According to recent reports, we used CD-HIT86 (v.4.8.1) and a 70% identity cutoff at the protein level to remove redundancy among the nearly 2 million RNApolA genes identified from the metagenomic survey. This step provided a database of 17,293 unique RNApolA proteins longer than 250 amino acids that encapsulate a wide range of cellular and viral diversity recovered from the metagenomic survey. Then, we used the phylogenetic workflow and visualization capabilities of anvi’o87,88 (v.8.1) using muscle89 (v.3.8.1551) and FastTree90 (v.2.1.11) to identify and remove RNApolA proteins corresponding to bacteria and plastids. Focusing on the 10,853 remaining unique RNApolA proteins, we iteratively used the same anvi’o (v.8.1) workflow of de novo alignment and tree reconstruction, but this time to identify and remove outlier sequences (isolated or long branch in the tree topology) to improve the overall quality of the tree, as commonly done in phylogenetic workflows (for example, refs. 30,91,92). A total of 13 iterations were performed, after which 8,672 unique RNApolA proteins remained. Using this curated database, we explored the phylogenetic signal of RNApolA proteins using taxonomic annotations and the novelty score for guidance. This led to the identification of a monophyletic clade corresponding to the egoviruses, which is most closely related to asfuviruses and poxviruses. We incorporated these sequences in our custom diamond (v.2.1.8) database and performed a second diamond blast on the nearly 2 million RNApolA proteins, to identify Egovirales RNApolA proteins (percentage identity more than 50%) and study their source scaffold. Data availability Item 01 provides all the RNApolA protein sequences, diamond blast databases, reference taxonomic information and fast-tree phylogenies described in this section and the previous one. This methodology recovered 12 complete Egovirales genomes.

Recent findings suggest that we collected reference culture genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) corresponding to Asfuvirales and Chitovirales, as well as few Megaviricetes representatives from the Giant Virus Database (GVDB) collection10. We added the 12 complete Egovirales genomes into this ‘Nucleocytoviricota genomic resource’ (Data availability Item 02) and used Orthofinder93 (v.2.5.5 in diamond_ultra_sens mode) to characterize gene clusters. Gene clusters occurring in at least 10 out of the 12 Egovirales complete genomes were labelled as ‘Egovirales core genes’ (n = 57). Finally, functional annotation was performed using HHpred94 profile–profile comparisons from the HH-suite v3 package against Pfam, Protein Data Bank, Conserved Domain Database and viral protein sequences (uniprot_sprot_vir70) databases available from the MPI Bioinformatics Toolkit95. Protein structures were modelled using AlphaFold2 (ref. 96) through a local installation of ColabFold97 (v.1.5.5). In the case of the DJR-MCP of Egovirales, ColabFold97 (v.1.5.5) successfully predicted its three-dimensional structure and confirmed the presence of the DJR protein components characteristic of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota (Data availability Item 03).

Recent findings suggest that among the Egovirales core genes (previous section), those occurring as a single copy in at least 10 out of the 12 complete genomes were labelled as ‘Egovirales single copy core genes’ (n = 51). Notably, single copy core genes can provide relevant estimates of completion and redundancy for egovirus genomes. Briefly, we built an HMM with HMMER82 (v.3.1b2) for each Egovirales single copy core gene and created a corresponding HMM collection ready to use within anvi’o (v.8.1) (Data availability Item 04). In following sections, the completion and redundancy of egovirus genomes was predicted by counting the hits from this HMM collection, as commonly done in the field of environmental genomics and previously applied to other viral lineages (for example, refs. 30,34).

It has been revealed that most nucleocytoviruses contain a few core genes most central to their functioning, which are related to a virion morphogenetic module (including the MCP) and an informational module (including DNA and RNA polymerases). These genes are referred to as hallmark genes (for example, refs. 10,30). We used hmmsearch (default settings) from HMMER82 v.3.3.1 to search HMM profiles previously designed for these eight hallmark genes30, and collected matching sequences of Nucleocytoviricota from the Nucleocytoviricota genomic resource (‘Functional annotation of Egovirales core genes’ section). Given that genomes of faustoviruses from the GVDB collection10 had partial DJR-MCP genes, we replaced those with seven strains of faustoviruses from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank collection (strains E9, LCD7, M6, S17, liban, vv10 and vv63; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/, accessed February 2024). We also added the Variola virus isolate VARV V563 genome from the Global Ocean Eukaryotic Viral (GOEV) database30, and replaced the Megaviricetes representatives initially picked from the GVDB collection with others in the GOEV database30 on the basis of their distribution as well as the occurrence of hallmark genes. In addition to the RNApolA and DJR-MCP protein sequences already recovered, we obtained sequences for the DNApolB, the second largest DNA-dependent RNA polymerase subunits (RNApolB), the transcription factor IIS, the D5-like primase (Primase), the poxvirus late transcription factor and the packaging ATPase. The DNApolB gene, often present on two separate open reading frames in egoviruses, required manual curation through BLASTp alignments (BLAST98 v.2.10.1) and phylogenetic reconstructions, as described in ref. 30. Briefly, when a single egovirus genome had two sequences for this gene, their positions were inspected in a maximum-likelihood single-protein phylogenetic tree, and their sequences were aligned with BLASTp to a close reference sequence and to each other. The two DNApolB sequences for a same egovirus systematically corresponded to a clear split: they were fused and accordingly labelled for further notice. The same protocol was performed for the RNApolA and RNApolB protein sequences, occasionally split in egoviruses. Finally, we created a database of 77 Nucleocytoviricota genomes containing at least 7 out of the 8 hallmark genes, for downstream single-protein phylogenetic analyses (Data availability Item 05).

From the genomic database created in the previous section (section ’Recovery of eight Nucleocytoviricota hallmark genes’), protein sequences corresponding to the same hallmark genes were aligned with MAFFT99 v.7.464 using the L-INS-i algorithm and default parameters. Sites with more than 70% gaps were systematically trimmed using goalign v.0.3.5 (https://www.github.com/evolbioinfo/goalign). The maximum-likelihood phylogenetic reconstructions were performed using IQ-TREE100 v.1.6.2, with the ModelFinder101 option to determine the best-fitting model. Supports were computed from 1,000 replicates for the Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood ratio (aLRT)102 and ultrafast bootstrap approximation (UFBoot)103. Supports were deemed good when Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like aLRT 80% or greater and UFBoot 95% or greater, as per the IQ-TREE manual and moderate when only one of the two conditions was met. The eight phylogenetic trees (Data availability Item 06, including protein sequences and trees) were visualized and rooted between the Megaviricetes and Pokkesviricetes classes using anvi’o (v.9.1).

We collected 20 DJR-MCP sequences from Egovirales source scaffolds (section ‘Phylogenetic signal pointing towards egoviruses’), which include the complete genomes. We aligned them using MAFFT v.7.464 (L-INS-I algorithm; default settings) and generated an HMM profile dedicated to the Egovirales DJR-MCP (Data availability Item 04) using hmmbuild (HMMER82 v.3.3.2). This HMM profile was then searched against all predicted gene sequences from the metagenomic database, using hmmsearch (HMMER82 v.3.3.1) and an E-value cutoff of 1 × 10−10. Positive hits (based on both RNApolA and DJR-MCP) were then linked back to their source scaffold, expanding the scope of Egovirales-positive metagenomic samples (Data availability Item 07).

The mOTUs database contains metagenomic bins generated using Metabat2 (ref. 104) (v.2.15) with differential coverage information, as described in refs. 76,77. Here we analysed all scaffolds of mOTUs containing signal for the RNApolA gene and/or DJR-MCP gene of Egovirales, along with other scaffolds occurring in their associated bins. From the 57 Egovirales core genes, we selected 42 that were highly specific to Egovirales compared with Asfuvirales, Chitovirales and Megaviricetes (that is, those genes often occur in Egovirales but rarely in other nucleocytoviruses), and created a collection of 42 HMMs extracted from the collection of 57 core genes (Data availability Item 04). Scaffolds lacking signal for any of those 42 HMMs were removed to only work on high-quality viral MAGs. After this removal step, we predicted the completion and redundancy of Egovirales MAGs using the HMM collection of Egovirales single copy core genes. Finally, we removed MAGs with a quality score (completion minus redundancy) below 50%. We processed the final genomic database (Data availability Item 08, which contains 224 Egovirales environmental genomes) with anvi’o (v.8.1) to predict gene sequences (with Prodigal81 v.2.6.3) and functionally annotated hallmark genes using specific HMMs. The Egovirales proteins were subsequently clustered into orthogroups using OrthoFinder (v.2.5.5, default settings), and orthogroup assignments were mapped to those from the initial functional annotation (section ‘Functional annotation of Egovirales core genes’). Finally, we used FASTANI105 (v.1.34) within anvi’o (v.8.1) to create a non-redundant database (less than 95% average nucleotide identity) of 116 Egovirales environmental genomes, 6 of which are human specific (Data availability Item 08).

We performed a multi-protein phylogenetic analysis of nucleocytoviruses on the basis of the concatenation of DNApolB (sequences of 100 amino acids or more), RNApolA (sequences of 200 amino acids or more), RNApolB (sequences of 200 amino acids or more) and transcription factor IIS protein sequences (sequences of 25 amino acids or more), as previously done in ref. 30. For Megaviricetes, we used manually curated hallmark genes from the GOEV database30 (excluding Medusavirus). For the Pokkesviricetes, we used the same resource as described in the section ‘Recovery of eight Nucleocytoviricota hallmark genes’ (genomes from the GVDB collection10 supplemented with faustoviruses from the NCBI GenBank collection and Variola virus from GOEV; Data availability Item 05) and the 224 Egovirales environmental genomes (Data availability Item 08). This phylogenetic analysis followed the protocol described in the previous section, except that the FFT-NS-i algorithm of MAFFT v.7.464 was used for the alignment of each individual protein dataset, before they were trimmed (sites with 70% or greater gaps, using goalign v.0.3.5) and concatenated. Supports were computed from 1,000 replicates for the Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like aLRT102 and UFBoot103. The phylogenetic tree (Data availability Item 06) was visualized and rooted using anvi’o (v.9.1).

Sources indicate that to go beyond the scope of environmental genomes (previous section), we performed global phylogenies containing all RNApolA (sequences more than 600 amino acids) and DJR-MCP protein sequences (sequences more than 600 amino acids) of egoviruses extracted from the metagenomic survey (Data availability Item 07), using genomes of asfuviruses and chitoviruses from GVDB as the outgroup. The phylogenetic trees were inferred using the same approach as for the single-protein phylogenies: the sequences were aligned using the L-INS-i algorithm of MAFFT v.7.464 (default settings), sites with 70% or more gaps were trimmed using goalign v.0.3.5 and the trees reconstructed using IQ-TREE v.1.6.2 and the ModelFinder option. Supports were computed from 1,000 replicates for the Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like aLRT102 and UFBoot103. The phylogenetic tree (Data availability Item 06) was visualized and rooted using anvi’o (v.9.1).

We generated a non-redundant database (average nucleotide identity less than 95%) of egovirus MCP genes, egovirus RNApolA genes and eukaryotic RNApolA genes characterized from the Egovirales-positive samples using CD-HIT86 (v.4.8.1) (Data availability Item 09). We performed read recruitment of all the Egovirales-positive metagenomic samples against the database. For that, quality-controlled metagenomic reads were mapped (Bowtie2, ref. 106, v.2.4.116) against the database and the ‘anvi-profile-blitz’87,88 (anvi’o v.8.1) routine used alignments to generate mean coverage values. Taxonomic information was included using the diamond blast (v.2.1.8) for RNApolA genes (section ‘Taxonomic affiliation of RNApolA sequences’) and the phylogenetic tree for MCP genes.

A global k-mer survey (k = 31) of the MCP, DNApolB and RNApolA single copy core genes of a genomic representative of the main human clade (MAG: ZEEV15_1_SAMEA3664761_BIN_00000011) was performed against the SRA data (at the assembly level) using the online tool Logan-Search107, with a minimum k-mer coverage of 50% (default Logan-Search cutoff to minimize false positives). This search provided 524 candidate-positive samples, comprising 270 with 3 markers, 95 with 2 and 159 with 1. Because the tool only allows screening of nucleotide sequences smaller than 1 kb, we only analysed the first 1 kb of these three genes.

Egovirales proteins (from the 224 environmental genomes), together with Pokkesviricetes (Asfuvirales and Chitovirales) from the GVDB collection and Megaviricetes from the GOEV collection, were used as queries for similarity searches against UniProt-TrEMBL using MMseqs2 (ref. 108) (v.17-b804f) with default settings. Hits not clearly assigned to cellular organisms were removed on the basis of taxonomic annotations (Supplementary Table 5). For each query, only the best hit with 30% or more identity and a minimum bit score of 100 was retained. Given the enrichment in Metamonada and Trichostomatia (Ciliophora) among hits for Egovirales proteins, the same queries were searched against further metamonad and ciliophoran genomes retrieved from NCBI Genome and the Genome Warehouse (list in Supplementary Table 8; Data availability Item 10 provides the corresponding proteomes) using identical parameters. Bit score values were used to compare the hits across the independent runs, and only the highest-scoring hit per query was retained. For functional overview, Egovirales proteins and their corresponding best hits in metamonads and Ciliophora were queried for searches against Pfam-A.full (release 38.0) using MMseqs2 (v.17-b804f; default settings), retaining only the best hit per query. To further assess the specificity of the detected similarities, we performed reciprocal similarity searches using all metamonad and ciliophoran proteins that matched an Egovirales protein (30% or greater sequence identity and bit score 100 or greater) as queries, irrespective of whether they represented the best hit for the original viral query. These proteins were searched against the Egovirales, Pokkesviricetes (Asfuvirales and Chitovirales) and Megaviricetes protein datasets using MMseqs2 (v.17-b804f) with default settings (Supplementary Table 8). They were also searched against UniProt-TrEMBL to identify proteins showing stronger similarity to homologues outside Nucleocytoviricota. When metamonad proteins were used as queries, UniProt-TrEMBL hits assigned to Metamonada were excluded to avoid self-matches to closely related strains represented in the resource. For each query, only the best hit within each target dataset was retained.

Recent findings suggest that our protein sequence comparisons identified a gene flux signal connecting egoviruses and two clades of eukaryotes: Parabasalia and Trichostomatia. Most of this signal was due to egovirus core genes occurring in the eukaryotic genomes. To clarify the directionality of this gene flux, we performed phylogenetic analyses for four egovirus core genes of known function (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase largest subunit (RNApolA), DNApolB, mRNA capping enzyme and Holliday junction resolvase) and two egovirus core genes of unknown function (OG0000040 and OG0000089). HMM profiles for the mRNA capping enzyme (PF03919.22) and Holliday junction resolvase (PF04848) were retrieved from the InterPro database (https://ebi.ac.uk/interpro/), whereas latest HMM profiles were constructed for OG0000040 and OG0000089 (those are core genes of Egovirales lacking any annotation) using hmmbuild (HMMER82 v.3.3.1) from Egovirales sequences aligned with MAFFT v.7.464 (FFT-NS-2 algorithm, default settings) (Data availability Item 04). Homologous sequences were identified using hmmsearch (HMMER82 v.3.3.1) with the profiles’ gathering threshold score cutoffs for the InterPro HMM profiles (default minimum bit score of 22 for Holliday Junction and 26.5 for mRNA capping) and default E-value inclusion threshold for the two others (E-value below 0.01), and collected from Pokkesviricetes, Megaviricetes and the set of extra Metamonada and Ciliophora (previous section), as well as from the TCS database (derived from EukProt v.3 and representing the diversity of eukaryotes109). To reduce redundancy for the mRNA capping enzyme and Holliday junction resolvase, sequences were clustered with CD-HIT (v.4.8.1) with dataset-specific thresholds (80% or more and 95% identity for TCS sequences in the mRNA capping enzyme and Holliday junction resolvase datasets, respectively; 90% or more identity for GOEV sequences in both gene families). For DNApolB and RNAPa, HMM profiles and cellular and/or viral homologues were obtained from ref. 30, and homologues from metamonads, Ciliophora and egoviruses identified using hmmsearch (HMMER v.3.1) were directly incorporated into these datasets. For the DNApolB, RNApolA and mRNA capping, sequences shorter than 100, 200 and 100 amino acids, respectively, were removed. In the case of DNApolB, we also removed sequences longer than 2,000 amino acids. Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v.7.464 (FFT-NS-2 algorithm, default settings), sites with 70% or larger gaps were trimmed using goalign v.0.3.5 and phylogenetic trees (Data availability Item 06) were reconstructed using IQ-TREE v.1.6.2 with the ModelFinder option. The alignment, trimming and tree inference process was iterated for some of the trees to identify and remove outlier sequences (isolated or long branch in the tree topology) before final inference to improve the resolution and stability (Supplementary Information and Data availability Item 06).

The KilA gene, which is associated with polinton-like elements in metamonads, especially parabasalids, was analysed separately due to its distinct evolutionary context. An HMM profile (PF04383.19) was retrieved from InterPro (https://ebi.ac.uk/interpro/) and used to identify homologous sequences across Pokkesviricetes (including egoviruses), Megaviricetes and Metamonada using hmmsearch (HMMER v.3.3.1, profile’s gathering threshold score cutoff). Considering the specific enrichment of polinton-like elements in Metamonada, extra genomes were included: T. vaginalis strains ATCC 30188 (GCA_002891335.1) and ATCC 50138 (GCA_052324655.1), T. tenax isolate Hs4:NIH (GCA_047301845.1) and strains NIH4 ATCC 30207 (GCA_900231805.1), Trichomonas gallinae isolate XT1081-07 (GCA_008369845.1), Trichomonas sp. genotypes 1c (GCA_047372395.1) and 2a (GCA_047372375.1), and Pentatrichomonas hominis isolate Hs-3:NIH (GCA_047301545.1). To limit redundancy, sequences from GOEV, GVDB and Metamonada genomes were clustered independently using CD-HIT (v.4.8.1; 95% or more identity threshold), and only the representative sequence of each cluster was retained (Data availability Item 11). To reduce the volume of eukaryotic sequences, all the sequences were used as queries in a similarity search against Pfam-A.full (release 38.0) using MMseqs2 (v.17-b804f; default settings); eukaryotic sequences without a best hit to KilA-N were removed. Remaining sequences were aligned using MAFFT v.7.464 (FFT-NS-2 algorithm; default settings), sites with 70% or greater gaps were trimmed using goalign v.0.3.5 and the phylogenetic trees were inferred using IQ-TREE v.1.6.2 with the ModelFinder option. Outlier sequences (isolated or long branch in the tree topology) were removed from the sequence dataset before a new iteration of de novo alignment, trimming and tree reconstruction was performed. A total of eight iterations (in addition to the initial tree) were completed (Supplementary Information and Data availability Item 06).

It has been revealed that putative genes for the genome of T. vaginalis strain G3 (GenBank reference GCA-026262505.1) were retrieved, including their functional annotation and predicted positions of polinton-like regions110. Genomic positions of Egovirales-like hits as well as KilA genes of type I and type II were mapped onto it. Finally, MCP genes matching that of Polinton-1_TV, a well annotated polintovirus from the same T. vaginalis strain G3 (ref. 28) collected from the REPBASE database (https://girinst.org/repbase/), were identified using MMSeqs2 (v.17-b804f) and default settings.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Sources indicate that databases our study used or generated include the following Items: (1) all the data related to our RNApolA global survey, (2) viral genomes used to define the Egovirales core genes, (3) the three-dimensional structure of the Egovirales DJR-MCP, (4) all HMMs produced in our study, (5) viral genomes with at least 7 hallmark genes used for single-protein phylogenies, (6) all phylogenies (with associated metadata) produced in our study (including the iterations), (7) Egovirales RNApolA and DJR-MCP proteins found in the metagenomic assemblies, (8) the 224 Egovirales environmental genomes, (9) non-redundant RNApolA (eukaryotic and viral) and MCPs found in the egovirus-positive metagenomic assemblies, (10) proteomes of Metamonada and Ciliophora included into our gene flux analysis and (11) and KilA proteins found in nucleocytoviruses and Metamonada. These items have been made publicly available at Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25398895)111. Data were collected from the mOTUs database76,77, GVDB10, the MPI Bioinformatics Toolkit94, NCBI GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/), the GOEV database30, UniProt-TrEMBL112, the Genome Warehouse (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gwh/), InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/), the TCS database109 and the REPBASE (https://girinst.org/repbase/). Source data are provided with this paper.
